payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=link+between+path-dependent+belief+updating+and+stable+preference+formation+in+reinforcement+learning+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7498039\", \"title\": [\"Belief Updating in Social Networks Follows Synchronous Averaging Rather than Reinforcement Learning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>From scientific collaborations to online communities, collective judgments emerge as individuals repeatedly revise their beliefs in response to one another. Whether this process produces accurate beliefs or merely consensus depends on how people combine private evidence with their neighbors' judgments. Two families of computational models make distinct assumptions: DeGroot models synchronously average available opinions, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) models update beliefs sequentially from neighbor-specific prediction errors. These accounts have not been directly compared in controlled social networks with repeated real-time interaction. We compared them using trial-by-trial choices from two previously published experiments involving 209 and 760 participants, respectively. Participants repeatedly revised predictions in networks differing in size and topology. We fitted unweighted and degree-weighted variants of both model families and compared them using random-effects Bayesian model selection. We then used simulations parameterized by the fitted models to assess network-level accuracy and consensus. In both datasets, a DeGroot variant had the strongest group-level model evidence, although the best-fitting rule varied across individuals. Network topology also mattered: unweighted DeGroot best explained behavior in most structures, whereas degree-weighted DeGroot was favored in the highly centralized Royal Family network. Simulations showed that DeGroot averaging generally generated more consensus than naïve sequential RL, while degree-weighted RL could achieve similar accuracy and consensus depending on the assumed information-sampling order. Topology further shaped collective outcomes: hub-dominated networks could reach high consensus despite relatively low accuracy. Exploratory simulations showed that increasing network size improved accuracy but reduced consensus, whereas increasing average degree improved both. These findings establish DeGroot averaging as a robust baseline account of belief updating in interactive networks and show how learning rules, sampling order, and topology jointly determine whether networks become accurate, consensual, or both.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7498039\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.30693/smj.2022.11.5.82\", \"title\": [\"Link Stability aware Reinforcement Learning based Network Path Planning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Along with the growing popularity of 5G technology, providing flexible and personalized network services suitable for requirements of customers has also become a lucrative venture and business key for network service providers. Therefore, dynamic network provisioning is needed to help network service providers. Moreover, increasing user demand for network services meets specific requirements of users, including location, usage duration, and QoS. In this paper, a routing algorithm, which makes routing decisions using Reinforcement Learning (RL) based on the information about link stability, is proposed and called Link Stability aware Reinforcement Learning (LSRL) routing. To evaluate this algorithm, several mininet-based experiments with various network settings were conducted. As a result, it was observed that the proposed method accepts more requests through the evaluation than the past link annotated shorted path algorithm and it was demonstrated that the proposed approach is an appealing solution for dynamic network provisioning routing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.30693/smj.2022.11.5.82\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 6, 30]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1017/9781009051873.017\", \"title\": [\"Partial Observations and Belief States\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009051873.017\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 5, 31]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2147/ppa.s48468\", \"title\": [\"The preference for an endoscopist specific sex: a link between ethnic origin, religious belief, socioeconomic status, and procedure type\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2147/ppa.s48468\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013, 9]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "3200d5dc1985e82115a702328e68100076d74de605e2990361472ef6605c90af", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7498039", "doi:10.30693/smj.2022.11.5.82", "doi:10.1017/9781009051873.017", "doi:10.2147/ppa.s48468"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7498039", "https://doi.org/10.30693/smj.2022.11.5.82", "https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009051873.017", "https://doi.org/10.2147/ppa.s48468"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}

article.body:
Our current work investigates how artificial systems manage their limited resources, a process we call metareasoning, which simply means thinking about thinking. We are observing how systems decide when to stop planning and start executing tasks. Recent recorded readings emphasize that optimizing this allocation is vital for system efficiency, especially when systems attempt to solve problems they identified themselves. [1, 7]

As an analogy, imagine you are a contractor building a house. If you decide halfway through that you want to move a load-bearing wall to make a larger room, you cannot simply tear it down without risking the entire structure. You need a specialized blueprint that accounts for the foundation already poured. In the same way, we are looking at whether autonomous systems can identify and modify their own foundational assumptions without causing their own internal logic to collapse. [2, 4]

Researchers are finding that larger reasoning models often use a technique called constructive expansion, where they grow their internal logic to incorporate new facts, rather than simply deleting old ones. This is a critical distinction from smaller models that may rely on destructive truncation, where they delete old rules to fit new ones. This helps them maintain stable, consistent reasoning paths as they learn. [2]

We are also examining how systems develop stable preferences over time. These preferences appear to be path-dependent, meaning they are shaped by the specific history of what a system has experienced, rather than being hardcoded facts. This suggests that how an agent is taught matters as much as what it is taught, because its future goals are anchored in its past encounters. [5, 10]

To keep this process accountable, the team is exploring ethics-based auditing. This involves assessing an agent's behavior against a set of predefined principles. Some research suggests that separating a system's memory, control, and cognition into distinct architectures can make the reasons for a decision more transparent, allowing observers to see exactly why a system chose a particular path. [6, 7, 8]

We have made progress in understanding autonomous discovery, where agents independently identify worthwhile problems. Using frameworks that categorize problems into formulation, representation, and evaluation, agents are beginning to tackle complex research questions in a way that mimics scientific investigation. This involves constant communication across defined architectural dimensions to ensure coordination. [9, 11, 12]

Despite these advances, we face significant uncertainties. We have yet to confirm if these autonomous systems can truly identify the deepest, foundational assumptions that guide their logic without external intervention. Can an intelligent system reliably surface and test these premises on its own, or will it always require an external auditor to ensure it has not veered into a logical trap of its own making? [3, 6, 8]

Summary

We are studying how computer systems think about their own reasoning. We want to know if they can change their starting rules safely. They often form habits based on their past experiences, which we call path dependence. Researchers are trying to keep this process safe by separating the parts of a system that think from the parts that remember. We still do not know if these systems can fully correct their own deepest mistakes without human help. You can check the Console for new updates on this progress.
article.lede: We are exploring how artificial systems navigate the tension between their original instructions and the new, self-generated problems they encounter while working.
article.lens: Investigating how systems manage resource allocation and goal formation, focusing on the threshold where autonomy meets foundational logic.
article.title: Mapping the Boundaries of Autonomous Inquiry
